query: Which material can be used for ductility, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Pure copper exhibits excellent ductility at room temperature due to its face‐centered cubic (FCC) crystal structure that allows for the activation of multiple slip systems, facilitating extensive plastic deformation.
generation.intervention: Standard room-temperature mechanical testing without additional alloying or thermal treatments
generation.conditions: Controlled room temperature under tensile loading
generation.mechanism: Activation of multiple slip systems in the FCC structure enables the material to undergo significant plastic deformation before failure
generation.predicted_outcome: Copper will display high strain-to-failure and maintain ductility as evidenced by a smooth stress–strain curve with visible plastic deformation prior to necking
generation.baseline: Ductility performance observed in other well-annealed FCC metals
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to pure metals with FCC structures and may not extend to copper alloys or conditions that favor alternative deformation mechanisms (e.g., high strain rates, low temperatures)
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative ductility values and strain rate dependency require further experimental validation, and additional factors such as impurities or processing history could influence behavior

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of tensile tests on annealed, high-purity copper samples at room temperature. Prepare specimens according to standard tensile testing protocols and measure the stress–strain response until failure.
measurements: Flow stress behavior throughout tensile deformation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the copper samples do not exhibit high ductility (e.g., strain to failure is significantly lower than expected for FCC metals) or if the deformation behavior deviates markedly from the expected smooth, plastic flow with multiple slip system activation, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.
